speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet asked in a starred question yesterday for the number of unemployed registered at national employment offices in Quebec, Canada and Montmagny. The figures released yesterday are released by the Department of Labour and the dominion bureau of statistics.
Yesterday the hon. member rose on a question of privilege to protest against certain figures which I supplied in answer to starred question No. 29. The hon. member's objection was that more recent figures were available than those provided, which were for September 21. I now wish to give the figures for registrations at the national employment service on November 7, which was not the date specified by the hon. member, it being November 1.
At the same time I should point out that these figures include a number of categories which extend beyond the definition of persons without jobs and seeking work, which is the basis of the dominion bureau of statistics figure. Registrations at national employment offices are derived from a count of applications on hand in every office at the close of business on a specified day. The count excludes registrations from persons known to have jobs and applying for other ones. Measures are taken to exclude persons who have secured work on their own since registration.

Privilege-Mr. Lesage
Nevertheless, I am informed that the figures inevitably include a number of persons who had found employment or who had left the labour force when the count was made. Although not all persons looking for work register at national employment service offices, all those who are seeking unemployment benefits, regardless of the length of time for which they may be out of work, must register for work.
Thus, Mr. Speaker, taken as a measure of unemployment, which was what the hon. member requested, these figures do not have the authority of the official dominion bureau of statistics figures of persons out of work and seeking jobs. For that reason they are not published as official unemployment figures.
In this connection I might add that it was the previous policy, as I imagine the hon. member is well aware, to release figures of national employment service registrations only for the dates specified in the official dominion bureau of statistics release. I have decided to change this policy, on the principle that hon. members of this house are entitled to any information which it is within the power of my department to provide. Therefore I will give the figures the hon. member requested, and better; I shall give them for November 7, 1957, as compared with November 8, 1956: for Canada, in 1957, 327,388; for November 8, 1956, 188,362; for the Quebec region, 1957, on the same date, 90,853; for November 8, 1956, 52,258; for Montmagny, November 7, 1957, 948; for November 8, 1956, 356. In the event the hon. member is interested, the figure for June of this year was 1,112.

speechtext: Order. May I say to the house that there is some confusion between what is a question of privilege and what is a point of order. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Justice. Has the minister any further information to give to the house with regard to developments at the Britannia mine?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):

subsubtopic: FURTHER STATEMENT ON REPORTED CLOSING DOWN OF HOWE SOUND COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to be able to report to the hon. member in reply to his question and to the house on the course of discussions which I have held in this connection.
I should like, first of all, to express appreciation of the fact that when they learned of the desire of the government to explore the possibility of keeping the Britannia mine in operation, the management decided to defer their decision on closure of the mine which otherwise would have taken place on November 19. As a result it became possible to explore the situation with some hope of success, and I know that this is appreciated by all parties concerned as well as by the government.

Inquiries of the Ministry
In Vancouver recently I had discussions with the mine management, at which time the implications of various alternative proposals were studied. I also had discussions with the union leaders. I proceeded to Victoria on Wednesday, where I had discussions with the provincial ministers chiefly concerned in the matter. At these last discussions the possibility of joint action on one or more of the various potential alternatives was explored. These discussions were most helpful.
I returned to Ottawa this morning and have made a preliminary report to my colleagues. The situation now is that this report is to be considered further, and further discussions are to be held here with company officials by whom the eventual decision, so far as the company is concerned, will have to be made. During these discussions the proposals which seem to have emerged from the earlier talks as having the greatest appeal and practicability will be further explored, together of course with any proposals or alternatives which may be advanced by the company.
It will be appreciated that in discussions of this kind, in which the dominion and provincial governments take part and in which a company and its men are directly involved, it is necessary to proceed by stages, with the result that it is not always possible to reach agreement or decision quickly. However, I wish to assure the house that this government is pursuing the matter just as vigorously as possible and is prepared to consider all practicable alternatives which may have a chance of forestalling the closure of the mine at this time.

Yesterday we had quite a discussion on this item, all of which was very interesting. The members of this house having so recently gone through an election campaign, their knowledge of procedure is fresh in their minds. I found, on reviewing the questions which had been asked and the suggestions which had been made, that they fell into two or three precise categories. With your permission, Mr. Chairman, I will answer a couple of these questions.
I should like to point out that most of the discussion which took place yesterday is the

I might just say, though, with regard to the fee which is allowed for enumerators, that amount was changed last year in an effort to provide a more satisfactory method of enumeration. This matter is now being reviewed by the chief electoral officer, as is the matter of the rate to be paid for the printing of the voters' lists.
With regard to the latter, it was said yesterday by more than one hon. member in this house that the rate was so low it was practically impossible to have the work performed in union shops. I do not know what the union rates are in other parts of Canada, but in my own city the work is performed in union shops. I do not believe, therefore, that particular statement could be taken as a general indication of conditions across the country. Nevertheless, whether the rate is sufficient or not, it is being reviewed by the chief electoral officer, who has the matter under serious consideration.
Most of the other items mentioned were connected with advance polls, courts of revision and so on. There was one statement made which I think calls for an answer. It was a statement by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond, I believe, who said it was possible for the armed forces to write on their ballots the name of the party they wished to support rather than the name of the candidate. If I understood the hon. member correctly and that was his statement, then he is misinformed; that is not correct.
Other than that, Mr. Chairman, I think there are no particular points which need to be answered at this time. I would suggest to hon. members that they might save their comments and their experiences and present them to the committee on privileges and elections when it meets next session.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
I was speaking at the adjournment hour last night, and I thought I would continue today. In connection with handling elections in northern areas I should like to say, as I think the minister and the house know, that a large number of the people who vote are Indians and Eskimos. These people have their homes. Their homes are usually in the bush. What they call their permanent residence is in the bush, whether it be a log house or a tent, and they have no permanent residence in the villages or towns
Supply-Secretary of State scattered through the north. They travel around the country trapping, fishing and hunting or working at jobs where there is work available. We also have, of course, a large number of white people who make their living by fishing, trapping, prospecting, logging or who are employed by water transportation companies, air lines or trucking companies. It is natural that these people must be away from their normal place of residence very frequently in pursuing their means of livelihood.
On June 10 last, at one poll at Fort Rae in my riding 74 people voted out of a total number of 221 on the list. At Fort Good Hope 65 voted out of 146 on the list; at Coppermine 24 voted out of 118; at Arctic Red River, 15 out of 46. At Bathurst Inlet I think there were two or three people who voted out of a total number of 50 or 60 on the list. The reason for this, Mr. Chairman, is that, in particular at Fort Rae, Fort Good Hope and Arctic Red River, the people at that time were in the bush. They live in the bush and they were out trapping muskrat and beaver. At Coppermine and Bathurst Inlet, just a short while prior to the election the Eskimos there moved into the barren lands where the cariboo was available.
As I mentioned last night, the handling of the election in the Yukon on June 10 last shows clearly that there is a need for advance polls, and a need for more polling divisions in the northern areas. It seems to me a shame that an election can be thrown out because people are interested enough to take the trouble to exercise their right to vote. I hope that our gracious minister will study this problem and will recommend amendments to the elections act which will rectify this situation.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext: I shall be very glad to bring the matter to the attention of the chief electoral officer.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the minister has answered in part one suggestion that I was going to make or one question that I was going to ask, but I suggest that it was a conditional answer. It has been the practice after every election to have the Canada Elections Act reviewed by a committee of the house in the light of the experiences obtained in that election. The hon. lady is perfectly correct, as far as my memory goes, in saying that does not always happen in the first session.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext: It very rarely does.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
Sometimes it happens in the second session after an election. However, she must be

Supply-Secretary of State aware of rumours that are appearing in the press. She must be aware of things that are said by the Prime Minister from time to time and which suggest that another election could come at any time, indeed that it might come before another session of parliament is held. I can only assume that this is a decision to be made by the Prime Minister and that the hon. lady does not know what is in his mind. However, it seems to me that it is appropriate to make the suggestion that if there is to be a review of the Canada Elections Act between the election of June 10, 1957, and the date of the next one it might be safer to have that review take place at this session.
This is not an indirect way of asking the hon. lady whether she knows when the election is to be; it is quite direct, if she is prepared to answer. However, I suggest in all seriousness that consideration should be given to that review being undertaken soon so that if there are any changes on which there is general agreement, those changes might be put into effect at an early date. After all, it is common knowledge that the chief electoral officer, shortly after the election of June 10, sent messages that might be called "alerts" to the returning officers across the country. It is also known that in a number of instances returning officers have already asked candidates and runners-up in the last election to supply names of enumerators for urban areas. All of these things suggest to me that if there is to be a review, it should be undertaken now rather than be put off to the time of a second session of the twenty-third parliament which conceivably might never be held.
In connection with returning officers to whom I have made reference, I should like to ask the Secretary of State whether there is in the mind of the government any intention to make any wholesale changes in the appointment of returning officers. I know there are some who are under the impression that the chief electoral officer appoints the returning officers in the various constituencies. The hon. lady knows that is not correct. They are appointed by the governor in council-or in other words by the cabinet- and they are communicated to the chief electoral officer who publishes their names and addresses in the Canada Gazette. As a matter of fact, he is required by section 8(4) of the Canada Elections Act to publish that list in the Canada Gazette between the first and the twentieth days of January in each year. At the present time, unless some have died or have withdrawn from the position for one reason or another, the returning officers are those who were named in January of 1957. I have no brief for any particular returning

officer. I am not suggesting that any returning officer should be replaced. But I think it is a proper question to ask whether those who are the present incumbents can assume that they will be continued or whether there is any intention on the part of the present government to make a change.
I was pleased that the hon. lady indicated that the question of the rate per line to be paid for the printing of the voters' lists is under review by the chief electoral officer. I am hopeful that this is the kind of change that could be made without an amendment to the act and if he recommends an increase in the rate per line, I trust that it will be brought into effect. From the information that I have from my own city of Winnipeg, both from employers and employees-that is from the management and from the trade union side-I can assure her that there were a number of trade union shops in the city of Winnipeg which felt that they could not take on this work this year at the rate that is now allowed.
There is one other subject on which I should like to say a few words even though it has been spoken to at some length. As a matter of fact, it is perhaps for that reason that I want to say this further word about it. I am delighted at the number of members who have expressed the feeling that the time has come to amend the act so far as advance poll privileges are concerned, particularly to widen the qualifications. As hon. members know, I presented a bill a number of times, in fact, there is one on the order paper right now-whether or not it will be reached, I do not know-suggesting that the privilege of voting at advance polls should be extended to any qualified voter who finds that he will be absent from his polling division on election day for any reason whatsoever. I may say frankly that I cannot see that there is any reason for any restriction. This is one of the issues where both the Canadian Labour Congress and the Canadian Chamber of Commerce take the same view and I hope that favourable consideration will be given to this change.
I should now like to call one more witness in support of the proposition that the advance poll should be extended to all who find that they will be away, even if they are away on vacation. My witness is a very important one and he is a very highly respected member of this House of Commons, one to whom I have already had the privilege of paying my personal tribute. I refer to the hon. member for St. Paul's, His Honour the Speaker.
The fact that the hon. gentleman is the Speaker means that he does not take part in the debates in this house. I would not want to quote something which he had written if

I was going to argue with him but I feel I am at liberty to quote something of his with which I am in agreement. I hold in my hand a very excellent piece of election literature put out by the Progressive Conservatives in the constituency of St. Paul's urging the reelection to this House of Commons of a gentleman referred to in this leaflet as "Roly Michener".
On the fourth page of this document I find some useful information which was made available to the electors of St. Paul's concerning election arrangements. One of these bits of information reads as follows:
If you are a commercial traveller, an airline pilot or stewardess, a railway employee or a sailor you may vote in the advance poll from nine a.m. to seven p.m. Thursday, Friday and Saturday, June 6, 7, and 8 (sorry, but Liberal government regulations will not permit advance poll for vacationers).

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
The
member for Peterborough is correct; he is right-that is the way the act reads as put on the statute books by the Liberals, but I do not forget the fact that when my bill was before this house last session it was supported by this party, by the Social Credit party, by the member for Mackenzie River who has just spoken and by one or two other Liberals but it was opposed by the Liberals in the main and by all the Conservatives who were present.
Now however one of the foremost Conservatives, indeed the first commoner, has had it put on record that he objects to the Liberal government regulations having denied advance polls to vacationers. I agree fully with what His Honour has said and I hope that although he is not now on the floor where he can argue with regard to these matters the government will pay attention to what he has said, when some of the rest of us bring it to the attention of the ministers across the way.
I therefore hope, Mr. Chairman, that the growing support for this proposal will result in action being taken at an early date.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to prolong this debate on advance polls and I think this is scarcely the time to do so. We may be able to take up the matter when the hon. member's bill is before the house. I would however just like to say that if my memory serves me well, without the legislation before me, the measure of the hon. member, while it provided for an advance poll 10 days before election it did not provide for an advance poll two or three days before election.
I could not help but think yesterday when the hon. member for Kootenay West was
Supply-Secretary of State speaking that his firefighters would have been out of luck because they did not know 10 days beforehand that they were going to be away fighting a fire, and a great many people who are absent for reasons other than the pursuit of their business also do not know that far ahead. I just make this comment in passing. With respect to the change in returning officers, I am sure the hon. member is quite familiar with the provisions of section 8 of the Canada Elections Act. I can only say to him that this is a law-abiding government; we intend to proceed according to the act unless and until that act is changed and it is not the intention of this government, during this particular session, to propose any change in the act.
With regard to the election date I am beginning to wonder, Mr. Chairman, just what goes on around here. Personally I am preparing for the next session of this parliament.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext: But after listening to the hon. member for Kootenay East, who represents the official opposition in this parliament, and now the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, who represents another group, I wonder if the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre would tell me-since he is in the house -whether the two of them are preparing to "gang up" on this government.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman I would just like to say a word or two with regard to the question of enumeration. I know of cases where a person has been enumerated, has received his enumeration slip and felt sure he was on the election list but when the preliminary list was printed and forwarded, perhaps to one of his friends he looked at the list, discovered he was not on it after all. This is in spite of the fact that his name was written on the list given to the returning officer by the enumerator and the mistake would have been made by the printer who, in checking it over, had left off this particular name.
That means that the person involved has to go either to the returning officer with the slip he has received and get a certificate saying he can vote, or else go to the revising officer. In some cases of which I know these people are cripples who could not walk upstairs and it has meant that they had to go themselves, taking this slip with them. Where it has been a question of going to a revising officer, of course, an affidavit can be taken but in many cases the mistake has not been discovered until it has been too late to adopt this method of correcting the situation. I am wondering if there is any way by which the slip shown to the deputy returning officer could be taken as authority to vote.

Supply-Secretary of State

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it is not supposed to be taken as authority to vote but I know that in some cases the privilege has been accorded to a person holding an enumerated slip. I might say however to the hon. member that the voter himself does not have to apply to the returning officer; it can be done by proxy. Someone can take it for him and procure a certificate enabling him to vote.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext: But generally they do not find out until a day or so before election, or perhaps a week ahead of time, and then it is too late.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext: No, they may take it right to the returning officer rather than a revision board.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext: Another matter which I mentioned was the question of stairs and I just wondered if the hon. minister could advise the chief electoral officer to ask the returning officer to try and locate polling booths in places where people do not have to climb a dozen or more stairs. I have heard of cases where ankles and legs have been broken in some places which are not very well lit and of course there is also the question of persons with heart conditions.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to bring forward a grievance before the minister which concerns the fishermen in my constituency who very seldom have the privilege of voting. We all agree I am sure that our people in Canada should have this privilege. We preach to them: Whatever you do get up and vote; it does not matter for whom you vote, but be sure to vote.
Now these fishermen have not had that privilege. It appears that the favourite time for elections is during some time in June and the fishermen from the districts of Riverton, Selkirk, Hnausa, Arnes, Gimli and Winnipeg Beach have to leave about the 29th or 30th of May. They must go to the fishing grounds which in some cases are about 200 miles away. Now the hon. lady may say to me "Well, what should I do about that?" Well, I would say "Extend the time for the advance polls." The last election was held on June 10 and these chaps had to be at the fishing grounds on June 6 so they did not get a vote.
I do not think anybody wants to do them out of a vote but I would like the hon. lady to see if she could get an amendment so as to enable an extension of the advance polls so that the fishermen in lake Winnipeg will have the right to their vote.
I think every good Canadian should vote, and these men complain bitterly to me about not having an opportunity. Election year after election year they have been deprived of the franchise. I am not going to take up

a lot of time, but I see in the papers that there has been an awful lot of telegraphing of votes going on in different parts of the country, and maybe we will be able to get the fishermen trained to radio in their votes.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, last evening
I was endeavouring to assist the Secretary of State inasmuch as I felt that many of the problems which were raised at that time might better be raised when the committee sits, and I want to assure the hon. lady that my prognostications were based on the warlike speeches and "brinkmanship" that were used by hon. members of the government party.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate
the answers given by the Secretary of State, but I regret that she did not answer-or at least I did not hear her answer-one of the questions which I raised yesterday, and one which is to me of the utmost importance. If the act is not going to be changed before the next election, cannot provision be made for putting the place where a person should vote in a more prominent position on the tear sheet? I hope the Secretary of State has not forgotten that question, and that something will be done about it.
I am not at all sure when the next election will be called-I have not the faintest idea- all I know is that last week I was notified from Vancouver that the returning officers in British Columbia have now received all the supplies which are required, and neither the Liberals nor the Socreds nor the C.C.F. group have anything to say in the sending out of supplies to the returning officers.
There is one other thing I should like to mention while I am on my feet-it is strictly my personal view, but I wonder whether the Secretary of State would give any consideration to it. In the years in which I had the privilege of being a member of the British Columbia legislature I noticed that in the estimates every year provision was made for a conference which dealt with what was known as uniformity of legislation, and that almost every session certain bills were introduced with regard to which members were told: there is no change in principle, this merely follows the recommendation of the nationwide conference to adopt uniformity of legislation. That brought this to my mind-that every five years, at the outside and, as a rule, every four years, every province in Canada has a provincial election. As far as British Columbia is concerned, for a few years they held one almost very year. So far as this house is concerned it is every four years; perhaps the time interval is shorter, but in any case it is not more than every five years that an election is held. This means the establishment of

voters' lists. Under federal legislation there has to be a brand new enumeration every time, a process which costs a lot of money; moreover, enumerations in every province of Canada must also cost a great deal of money.
Has any thought ever been given, or will it be given, to the advisability of establishing, along the lines of uniformity of legislation, a uniformity of eligibility to take part in elections both federal and provincial, and to the maintenance of a continuance up-to-date voters' list available at any time for use in a federal or provincial election, or in the event of a by-election?
I have thought this matter over for quite a few years, and although I recognize that certain technicalities might cause some difficulty I do not think it is impossible to establish uniformity of eligibility and a permanent record of voters which would be available for use in an election anywhere in Canada at any time. I am confident that if this were done hundreds upon hundreds of thousands of dollars would be saved to the taxpayers of this country, and to our provincial and federal governments. I should just like to throw out that suggestion now, and hope consideration may be given to establishing a system in Canada along the lines I have suggested.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I shall be very glad to bring the matter to the attention of the chief electoral officer, and I am sure that when the committee meets he will be glad to hear representations from the hon. member for Vancouver East on this interesting subject.
With reference to the remarks about the place of polling, I must say I find myself in complete agreement with the hon. member for Vancouver East. I have had exactly the same experience as he, and I have found that even in our own committee rooms many of our workers fail to see the location on the preliminary lists. I will consult with the chief electoral officer to determine whether or not he can suggest to the returning officers that this information be printed in larger type. Hon. members will notice that it does appear now in bold-faced type-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
But
only in 8 point type.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext: But still small.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
Oh yes, it is small. It seems to me that it could be in much larger type to draw immediate attention to it and, as I say, I will be glad to draw that matter to the attention of the chief electoral officer. I do not think the mechanics of this proposal are a matter of any great difficulty. I believe
Supply-Secretary of State all that is necessary is to make the suggestion to the returning officers, and it could easily be carried out when they place printing orders.
With reference to the assertion that supplies have already gone out, these are the preliminary supplies, and it is the usual thing that is done after every election. The same procedure is gone through by the chief electoral officer in each case.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
As far as printing the place of voting on the voters lists is concerned, I want to draw the attention of the Secretary of State to the fact that there is quite a difference in each constituency depending on the particular printer used by the returning officer. In some constituencies the voting place is printed in the same type as other reading material printed alongside of it, but in others printers will set it up in bold-faced type which stands out clearly. This seems a matter which could easily be corrected by a directive from the chief electoral officer, within the scope of the present legislation, and that no additional legislation is needed.
As to the committee of the Canadian Bar Association dealing with uniformity of legislation, I am not aware that this subject of a uniform election act has come before this body. It is probably something which should be suggested to them for consideration, because it will certainly be a great convenience if the election acts of the provinces and of the federal government were similar in their main points. One of the main reasons for this being desirable is that the officials appointed under the federal act very often draw on their experience and knowledge of the provincial election acts and, consequently, you get practices which are perfectly fair as between the parties but which are quite offensive as far as the federal election act goes. These practices are entered into in good faith by the election officers concerned, so I do hope that the Secretary of State will look into this matter to see whether something can be done along the lines of getting uniformity of election acts, at least with regard to the main points. It is a matter that I imagine would take some time. I do not think it could be done quickly but I do wish the minister would take it into consideration.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, what I have to say is very close to what the minister had to say in some of her answers. While she is considering this matter of absentee voting I am sure she will be interested to know-and I give this as an illustration-that one of the fishermen in my riding indicated to me that the last election was the first time he had had a vote since the war. It just so happened that he was not in port on the day on which

Supply-Secretary of State the previous elections were held. Unless they are in port it makes it practically impossible for them to vote. A broadening of the advance poll regulations would certainly be worth while. The fishermen are not included today. If they were included the crew would have the opportunity to vote.
I am particularly interested in another class on which I did not hear the minister comment. I must admit I was not here at all times. I refer to the pay that is given to the enumerators, namely 10 cents a name.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext: I did comment on that.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext: Yesterday?

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext: No, today.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext: I am sorry; I missed it. I wonder whether the minister would repeat it.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, what I said was-and the hon. member is aware of this-there was some change in the remuneration in the last election. Although the per-name rate was maintained, a minimum was established in an effort to secure a more efficient enumeration. Now, in some instances I understand the new rates did not work out as well as had been expected but I can assure the hon. member that the chief electoral officer is considering it very carefully.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have one item I should like to draw to the attention of the minister. It has to do with the use of schools as polling locations. In the last election the Vancouver school board made the schools available at the request of one returning officer and they then broadened their permission to include schools throughout the city.
The schools are used in municipal and provincial elections in British Columbia. In those schools you have not the problem of stairs. The location is well-known to all of the residents in the area. They are used to going there and voting. The surroundings have a dignity to them that you do not get in the ordinary polling places. It worked out very satisfactorily but only one returning officer in all of Vancouver took advantage of the offer of the Vancouver school board. They are considering whether, when the next election comes along, they might not even close down their schools for two or three hours. They do not need to do that because you can use the gymnasium or the auditorium and set up as many as 10 to 12 polling stations in the one location.
The one returning officer to whom I am referring is permitted to hire special constables. Well he hired one for about 10 polls. That man acted to direct traffic. I visited as many polling stations as I could on election day and the business of the day was being con-

ducted in those schools and in those multiple polling areas much better than in the individual homes. I do not understand why more use has not been made of such public facilities by the electoral officers. It seems to me to be a sensible and a wise way of handling it and I would commend it to the minister.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I listened with keen interest to what the hon. gentleman just said and I should like to support him very strongly in the remarks he has made. I have particular reference to what happened in the constituency of Laurier during the last election day on June 10. I am not free to speak of those irregularities which took place -I would like to-because there is an investigation taking place at the present time; but I am sure that had the polling stations been established in a school, in a gymnasium, or in some other public hall, it would not have been possible for those irregularities to have taken place.
I have discussed the matter with the returning officer in the constituency and I think he, too, is of the view that consideration should be given by the chief electoral officer and by the minister as well, I am sure, to this suggestion. It would avoid those irregularities and it would avoid people going into the polling booth in groups, particularly when the polling booth is in a small room of a house. I think there is a great deal to be said in favour of it. There have been irregularities, not only in my constituency, but in other constituencies elsewhere in the province of Quebec, and it does strike me that this would be an excellent suggestion which the minister should take into consideration and give careful study to.
If I understand the act correctly, I believe it is the responsibility of the returning officer to make a recommendation to the chief electoral officer who afterwards decides whether in his judgment and in the circumstances existing in the particular riding it is appropriate to have the polling stations in a public building of some sort. But I do want to go on record as supporting to the fullest extent that kind of suggestion and I trust the minister will give it the consideration it deserves.

maintopic: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think we all agree with the remarks of the hon. member for Laurier and the hon. member for Vancouver South. I think it is fair to say that the practice which they wish to correct has already been corrected in some ridings in this country. I know that within my experience the returning officer that I have to work with in my constituency has almost invariably- as far as I know invariably-picked a public

place when a public place was available at a convenient location. It is the normal practice in a village, town or hamlet that the polling place is in the community hall. Out in the country, if there is a schoolhouse available at a central location, the polling place is usually in the country school. I think it is a good practice. I agree with the support that has been given to this idea.
As far as my own constituency of Assini-boia is concerned, my returning officer, Jack W. O'Neil, of Viceroy, Saskatchewan who was appointed by the previous administration, has done a very good job. There is one practice that I think we all agree has grown up. The enumerators and clerks in rural polls, and the other officials in urban polls, have been appointed almost solely-at least to a large extent-on the basis of the party which they have supported. In the past the returning officer has appointed people who have supported the Liberal party. I do not think that is a good practice; I do not think it is a necessary practice and I do not think it is of any political advantage to the party in power. The general instructions which go out to the returning officers today, when they are finding officials to carry on this very important duty, should be to obtain the services of the people who can do the best job and not to give them first of all a blood test to find out how they voted in the previous election.
I am hoping that under the new government there will be a change in attitude. In my own constituency there will have to be because I do not think there were sufficient supporters of the present administration in the last election to man all the polls. Therefore, there is a very real opportunity to pick all these people on the basis of the job that they can do. I would ask the minister to take that into consideration. I do not think Canadians today appreciate, or approve generally, the attitude that you have to be a supporter of the government in power before you can obtain any of the small jobs as far as pay is concerned, but very important jobs as far as the welfare of our country is concerned and the proper functioning of the democratic system.
I go along with those who have said that there must be changes in the election act in order that the thousands of people who are now disfranchised in elections will get the vote. Mention has been made many times-it is not necessary to repeat it-that many people are away from home on election day and that the provision as to people who may vote at advance polls is far too restricted. As I see it, the mere extension of the qualifications with respect to people who may vote at advance polls is not going to do the full job
Supply-Secretary of State in probably half of the ridings in the country. The experience we have had is that there are very few advance polls in rural ridings and if a person is eligible to vote at an advance poll he may have to travel 50 or 100 miles to reach that poll.
Therefore the mere extension of the qualifications in regard to those who can vote at advance polls so that more people may vote is not going to meet the situation fully. It might help to provide a great many more advance polls. Along with the suggestions that have been made, it would seem to me that the various election acts should be as uniform as possible. The government should be aware that in a growing number of provinces people now are able to vote by absentee ballot in a provincial election and when a federal election comes along they are completely confused. They have had a chance to cast their ballot in a provincial election if they are away from home. When a federal election comes along they assume they have the same privilege. They have probably been somewhat careless but the result is that they are not able to vote. They are not able to obtain a copy of the election act in order to study it. They assume they will have the same rights and they are disfranchised.
But there is a particular group that I think should be given special consideration. I think it is a shame that provision is not made for patients in hospitals to vote on election day. I think it is a shame that people who have to go to hospital after the writs are issued are disfranchised. Surely some special consideration should be given to this problem. People do not go to hospitals for fun and they should be given the chance to vote. There are polling stations in some hospitals but that does not mean that the patients who have to enter hospital after the writs have been issued can vote. The hospital polls are for the staff, the people who are ordinarily resident in that area, in the same way as any other poll. Therefore I ask that special consideration be given to people who are patients in hospitals.
There may be difficulties in providing an absentee ballot such as we have in some of the provinces whereby on election day a person can walk into any polling booth anywhere in the province, ask for a ballot, receive it and vote in his own electoral district. It seems to me that consideration should be given to providing that a person qualified to vote at one poll in an electoral district may cast his ballot in any other poll in that electoral district. The problem would not then be encountered of people changing from one electoral district to another and I think that

Supply-Secretary of State a great majority of the people otherwise disfranchised would be given the chance to cast their vote.
Will the Secretary of State assure the house that these points and others will be given consideration by the government? I do not imagine anyone present today knows precisely when the next election will be. I think there should be a committee at this session but if there is not going to be one then I point out that we are in a committee now where suggestions have been made and I hope that consideration will be given to those suggestions and that appropriate amendments to the act will be introduced.

I should like to make a few remarks on the subject which is now before us. I certainly agree that we need some amendments to the Canada Elections Act, especially with respect to the extension of the advance poll. I think we might well consider a far larger group of electors who should qualify in this field. Further, I think that we could probably handle our active hospital vote in this way. The hospitals for the chronically ill are as a rule subdivisions in themselves. The active hospitals are not as a rule and they have listed there only the interns and the staff. But if we were to make provision for an advance poll, I am sure that even in large municipalities where a hospital may be located at a boundary line the returning officers in two different ridings or even three different ridings could set up an advance poll in those hospitals.
Furthermore, I think we should also consider the possibility of making some change in the appointment of deputy returning officers and clerks so as to have it compare in a way with the set-up which we have for enumeration which works, in my opinion, very well.
With regard to the posting of voters' lists on trees and poles, I do not know whether or not this is the most satisfactory arrangement. In the city of Toronto, in municipal elections in the past it has been the practice to post the voters' lists in schools, fire halls and other public institutions. During the past year we have made further amendments in order to allow those lists to be posted on poles. I think we might well consider the possibility of adding to the advertising of the voters' lists by putting them in the post offices and schools as well as in the present locations. It was my experience in the past campaign that in some cases no sooner were lists posted than they were down the next day. I would think that furthering this objective of advertising voters' lists might be in the best interests of getting more people on the voters' lists without the last-minute flurry. These are the few observations that I wanted to make at this time. I hope that some of the other suggestions which have been made by other hon. members will also be taken up by the proper committee and be given due consideration.

Mr. Chairman, I had hoped that the minister would avail himself of this opportunity to report to the house on the activities of his department. I understand however that the estimates of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys were prepared by the previous administration, and this naturally accounts for the brevity of his remarks. Still, I am pleased to note that the minister has had no comment to offer on the remarks made by his colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming). The latter had stated that there had been an enormous amount of waste and extravagance in government departments. The fact that the minister has had nothing to say shows that, in his department at least, there has been no evidence of either waste or extravagance.
Mr. Chairman, I have a few remarks to make with regard to the mining industry. However, before going any further, I would like to offer my warmest congratulations to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Comtois) for the great honour which has come his way. He is now at the head of a very important department and I wish him every success. I know that he will grant every request we may have to make of him.
(Text) :
Mr. Chairman, I was hoping, too, that the minister would take this opportunity to give us a more complete answer to the question I put to him on October 16 regarding the amendment of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. I was hoping that the minister would announce that the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act was to be amended so as to make it more profitable for gold mines to operate and thus more profitable to the gold miners, to the small property owners in the mining communities and to those who are dependent on this industry.
I should like to take this opportunity also to tell the minister that he is very lucky to be in charge of such a department as the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, because he has under him a group of men and women who are devoted, who are very able and I know they will facilitate his work.

In the past the heads of the different branches of the department have done some excellent work. Their employees have done whatever they could to improve the services of this department. Therefore, I wish to pay tribute to them for their devotion to the mining industry.
Not very long ago an important event took place, Mr. Chairman. From September 8 to October 9, 1957 Canada played host to the sixth commonwealth mining and metallurgical congress. In fact, we were hosts to an imposing group of mining people from 35 different countries. To show the importance of this congress I think it would be appropriate for me to read what was published about it in the Northern Miner of October 17:
As a means of showing Canada's mining skills and wares to the world-to say nothing of displaying her scenery, her vastness, and her varied resources-it was an unqualified success. We doubt if any industry in any country has ever had a finer opportunity to place itself under scrutiny. Visitors from all over the world saw Canadian mining in wide perspective. They were able to see its diversity, observe its magnitude, study its enterprise, and evaluate its potential.
The article goes on to say:
We think, however, that the congress did more than all this. While primarily a Canadian exposition, it permitted many people from many countries to meet each other, to exchange ideas, to compare notes and problems. Everyone on the tour learned much about Canada, of course, but it is a good guess that he learned much about many other countries, as well. Such a growth of acquaintanceship can work wonders in the spreading of understanding, the establishment of friendships, and the deepening of international appreciations.
The sixth commonwealth mining and metallurgical congress did not just happen. It resulted from many months of planning and hard work by a great many enthusiastic workers on many committees in many places. To all of them goes unlimited credit for a task that was ably accomplished.
I wish to say here, Mr. Chairman, that some of those who worked hard on organizing this congress are precisely those who are on the personnel of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. Then, many other organizations did some good work in making this congress a real success. For myself, I had the pleasure to attend one of the meetings of the congress and I can say I was surprised to see the size of it and to see the interest in our mining industry of those who were visiting Canada.
There are other questions on which I should like to say a few words. I should like to deal mostly with the present situation in our mineral production. There are some soft spots in mineral production in Canada, and I am sure that when we see the statistics at the end of the year we will find that mineral production has suffered a substantial setback. The volume of mineral production for 1957 will be down not only in value but in physical 96698-88J
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys volume as well. In 1956 the total production amounted to $2,068 million and the physical volume had increased by nearly 275 per cent as compared with 1935. There will be a substantial decrease and, of course, the decrease will be mostly in the metallics division.
If hon. members will look at the statistics for the end of July-these are the latest statistics we have on the production of Canada's leading minerals-they will find that the production of copper is down in 1957; the production of gold, lead and zinc is down and the production of silver is also down. By the end of the year we shall find that for the first time since 1946 the total value of the production and also the physical volume of production will be down.
We have a special problem in the lead and zinc producing industry. At noon today I read an article in the Financial Post of November 23 which was entitled:
Canada Looks Like Losing U.S. Lead Tariffs Fight
I am afraid that within the next few months the zinc and lead producers in the United States may succeed in convincing the special tariff committee of the United States to increase the tariff on zinc and maybe establish quotas. Of course, in this matter the President of the United States has the last word and I hope he will not permit this increase in tariff because it would be very detrimental to the industry in Canada.
The zinc and lead producing industry in our country is a very substantial one. In the production of zinc Canada ranks second only to the United States. Of course, the largest producers are in British Columbia. The second largest producer is the Flin Flon mine in Manitoba. Lead and zinc mines producing ores and concentrates are also found in Quebec, Ontario, New Brunswick and Newfoundland. The trouble with the industry right now is the low price for zinc and lead, especially for zinc. The price is 10 cents a pound in the United States and Canada and 1 think it is only 81 cents in the United Kingdom.
This is a difficult situation and if on top of this low price the United States decides to impose tariffs on zinc, which may be as much as 2 cents plus per pound, the industry will be in a very difficult situation. It is estimated that already Canada has shown cooperation with the United States. The mines in the United States complain that Canada is exporting too much lead and zinc to that country but this is not a fact. We have cut down our exports to the United States by a substantial amount. We may not have cut down our exports of zinc but we have reduced our production. I am told that it is estimated that cut-backs, closures of mines which were forced to close on account of the low price and a general decline in production will

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys account for a 20 per cent reduction in production compared with 1956. This will mean a loss of production of some 80,000 tons of zinc during 1957.
Therefore we are hoping that the President of the United States will see his way clear to veto the decision of their tariff commission and that the tariff will not be increased so that our mines will at least be able to continue on a reduced scale in the production of refined zinc and zinc concentrates. If the president cannot do anything or if he is forced to agree with the tariff commission and increase the tariff, I think our government should look into the matter very carefully and maybe do something. Of course, I do not think that to retaliate against the United States, as was suggested, would be a good thing, but on the other hand if our lead and zinc industry is to suffer to the point that many of the mines have to close then I think something should be done.
It is a fact that many United States smelters depend on concentrates mined more particularly in the eastern part of Canada, in Quebec, Ontario and Newfoundland, in order to operate. Therefore I ask myself if it would not be wise for the government to study the proposal of encouraging the construction of a smelter in the eastern part of Canada in order to take care ourselves of our own concentrates. A very small quantity of concentrates is shipped overseas. I do not think any is shipped to the United Kingdom. We ship refined zinc to the United Kingdom, and if we were to refine more of our own zinc maybe we could find markets elsewhere in order to dispose of part of our zinc production.
I understand that this is a difficult problem because there is overproduction in the world having regard to the amount of consumption. Therefore there have to be cutbacks and some low-grade mines may have to close. On the other hand, it is very important that most of our mines be kept in operation. Moreover, in spite of the fact that we have overproduction I say that we should keep on looking for new mines.
During the last few months a discovery was made about 90 miles north of Senneterre, Quebec, and it would look as though there is a large deposit of zinc, lead, copper, silver and gold. It looks very much like the deposit will contain around 12 per cent zinc, one per cent copper, one or two ounces of silver and a few dollars in gold per ton. It would be very unfortunate if such a large deposit were left there unmined. The mining of the ore would probably provide a considerable amount of work for many men because actually the situation is the same in northern Quebec and northeastern Ontario as was

explained to us the other day by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano with respect to the Britannia mine in British Columbia.
Today we had a report by the Minister of Justice about the situation of the Britannia mine. Here is a mine that has the ore, a mine with the organization to keep itself in operaticn. If the mine closes those people will have to move. I think these problems are quite serious and I hope that the government will give consideration to what was suggested by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano and other members on all sides of the house who are interested in this particular mine in British Columbia.
It is important, as I said a few minutes ago, that we continue to search for new mines because if we wait until we need the product it may be too late. I think the United States are making a mistake by trying to force some of the Canadian mines to curtail their operations and search for minerals. We all remember quite well that during the war we were asked to produce more copper, more zinc and more lead, and that even during the Korean war we were asked to increase our production. I hope that these points will be taken into consideration by the United States government when they have to decide whether or not they will increase the tariff and impose import quotas.
I should like to refer to another industry which is classified under the fuels division. I read an article about oil production and apparently oil production is going at a slow speed in Alberta. In the Financial Post of November 2, 1957 there is the following:
On the oil and gas front-Crude oil nominations in Alberta for November dropped to 289,618 barrels daily-first time since May, 1955 that nominations have slipped below 300,000 barrels a day.
I am not an expert on oil but I understand that those who are experts expected that production would increase during 1957 and they were predicting a very high rate of production for 1958. Apparently the production in 1958 will not be much higher than that of 1957. These are some of the problems with which the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys should be concerned.
I understand that the matter of tariffs is properly the business of the Minister of Finance. Nevertheless, it is the duty of the department of mines to see that the industry is healthy, and the minister could and should make suggestions to the Minister of Finance to ensure the healthy state of this industry.
In so far as the copper industry is concerned, of course the price of copper came down and yesterday I think it was 27 cents in the United States and 25 cents both here and in the United Kingdom. Some mines have experienced difficulty in selling their

copper at even 25 cents and have had to accept a lower price. This is not a matter about which the government can do much because it is governed by demand. Nevertheless, it is tragic in a way to note that some of the mines have closed down. It is tragic also to see prospecting and the search for new copper mines declining. The companies are spending less money for exploration. This is not a good thing. It is not a good thing for us and it is not a good thing for our neighbours to the south. Our neighbours to the south are finding that their reserves of minerals are low, in all minerals except perhaps oil and coal. This situation is especially true of the metallic division.
Some day the United States will be coming to us for minerals. We know that the United States companies have invested large amounts of money here and those companies have engaged in prospecting and exploration. Now, however, our friends from the south are trying to hurt the Canadian mining industry, especially in the way I mentioned earlier, and they should not do that if they want to continue to be on a friendly basis with us. They should be very careful what they are doing.
I do not wish to take too much of the time of the committee, but I cannot allow this occasion to pass without speaking about the difficult situation in which the gold mines find themselves. I feel that the proper time to say something about this is during the consideration of the estimates of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. If I say something about the gold mines, I do so on behalf of the gold miners, the ordinary working men and businessmen, the property owners in all the mining communities in Canada. I have a number of mining communities in my own constituency. There are many such communities in the constituency of Timis-kaming and in the constituency of Timmins. There are some in British Columbia, some in northwestern Ontario and some in Manitoba. When I say that more help should be given to the gold mines, I am speaking on behalf of the people who live within those communities or in the smaller communities near large centres.
In northwestern Quebec, and the same situation applies in northeastern Ontario, if it were not for the mining industry there would be very little left for those who wished to work and to continue to live in those sections of our country. There would be the lumbering operations, but they are seasonal. The mining industry is the main industry in this part of our country. In the past, parliament has, as a whole, always endorsed whatever amendments or extensions were introduced to the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. I have heard so much from the
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys Minister of Finance, when he was on this side of the house, in support of the gold mines that I feel we should not be too worried. On the other hand, on October 16 when I put a question to the minister of mines he said that he and the Minister of Finance had received a delegation, and with the officials of the department were exploring ways and means of increasing the benefits under the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. Although the minister did not use those words he could not be considering decreasing the benefits so I deduced that the government is thinking of increasing the benefits under that act. Since that time we had not heard anything and the people in all parts of the country who are concerned with the gold mining industry are very anxious to hear from either the minister of mines or the Minister of Finance as to what is going to be done to help the gold mining industry.
The other day the hon. member for Timmins said something that I did not like very much. He implied that now somebody would be talking for the gold miners and the gold mining communities. I can tell him that if he reads the speeches I made during the last eight years he will find I never missed an opportunity to speak for the gold miners and the gold mining communities, as did many other members in this house. When we speak of the industry, naturally we speak of the gold mines, but when we are asking for some help we are asking that help for the gold miners and the gold mining community.

Mr. Chairman, I know the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Dumas) will forgive me if I do not follow up the excellent speech he has just given on the mining industry in his constituency.
I am very glad to take part in this discussion on the first item of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, and take this opportunity to congratulate the minister, not only on his appointment to the post which he occupies at this time but also for the courtesy he shows towards hon. members in his answers to their questions and in his general attitude towards them. I might add that some of his colleagues would profit greatly by following his example.
(Text) :
I should like at this stage, sir, to take advantage of your presence in the chair to tell you how pleased I was with your appointment, and to congratulate you and wish you well in the new honour which has fallen to you. I pause for a moment to do that because

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys you and I were next door neighbours for a period of many, many years as members of this house. I want to take advantage of the opportunity when you are in the chair to tell you sincerely, notwithstanding anything that might have happened in the house either recently or over the many years which I have been a member of the house, that I hold you in the highest esteem. I am very happy to see you occupying the position which you now hold.
I rose, Mr. Chairman, to deal with a question which, to me at least and I am sure to many other hon. members whom I will mention in a moment, is of the utmost importance. I refer to the demarcation of the boundary line between the southerly limits of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec on lake St. Francis. This is an old and vexatious problem. It is an old problem because it has existed over 40 years. It is a vexatious one because it has been the cause of a great deal of difficulty to those people who reside on both sides of an imaginary boundary line.
The hon. member for Stormont, my predecessor, has referred to this question on a number of occasions. He has shown a keen interest in it by the questions which he has asked. I am sure he has contributed in no small measure to bringing the question to the attention of the house and that is perhaps about all that can be done.
Along with other hon. members who are familiar with the British North America Act I realize that it is not within the jurisdiction of the minister to settle the question. But nonetheless, I think the minister is in a position,-for the reasons which I will give in a moment-because of the position which he holds, to use his influence or that of his department to bring to the attention of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec this matter which is causing great concern to the people of both provinces who live on either side of the boundary line.
The department over which the minister presides I think has a particular interest, first because of the fact that in that area there lies large numbers of islands, the property of the federal government in trust for the Indians and it is not possible to know in what area, either Quebec or Ontario, these islands are.
Another important reason which I think should interest the federal government is the fact that the St. Lawrence seaway authorities have given no less than $6 million worth of contracts, numbering about six or seven, for the deepening of the St. Lawrence seaway in lake St. Francis, which contracts are now in the course of being executed and where it is impossible to know whether the work being done is in the province of Ontario or in the

province of Quebec. Hence it is a ridiculous position for another crown agency to be in.
If I may, I should like to take just a moment or so to give a quick historical background of the situation. It was in the year 1914, more than 40 years ago, when a trapper was apprehended by a Quebec game warden on a place called Ross island. The Quebec game warden maintained that the trapper was in contravention of the law of the province of Quebec. In other words, he maintained that the island was in the province of Quebec. The game warden went on to state that he had authority to lay a charge under the game and fisheries act of the province against the trapper. It was at that time that the authorities of both provinces began to look into the question, and here is what took place.
Evidently they went back to the original statutes which existed. I hold in my hand the first one or at least one of the earlier ones. I should not say it is the first one because it is not. It is 52-53 Victoria, chapter 28, an imperial statute entitled the Canada (Ontario Boundary) Act. It was passed on August 12, 1889. It goes on to say this:
And whereas such boundaries, so far as the province of Ontario adjoins the province of Quebec are identical with those fixed by the proclamation of the Governor General issued in November, one thousand seven hundred and ninety-one, which have ever since existed:
And one of the clauses of the act reads as follows:
2. It is hereby declared that the westerly, northerly and easterly boundaries of the province of Ontario are those described in the address set forth in the schedule to this act.
Hence even from this early statute of 1889 it is clear that the northerly, westerly and easterly boundaries of the province of Ontario are established but that the southerly boundary which is along lake St. Francis was never delineated. One must therefore go back to the statutes of Upper Canada and the statutes of Lower Canada in order to ascertain where that boundary resides. The Consolidated Statutes of Upper Canada, 14 and 15 Victoria, chapter 4-5, section XI, reads as follows:
The limits of the townships in the county of Glengarry shall in like manner extend to the middle of lake St. Francis, and to the middle of the main channel of the river St. Lawrence, but shall also include all the islands not herein otherwise provided for, the whole or the greater part of which shall be comprised within the outlines of the said townships so prolonged.
The corresponding statute for Lower Canada, which is chapter 75, section 62, of the Consolidated Statutes of Lower Canada, reads as follows:
The county of Huntingdon shall be bounded . . . on the north by the river St. Lawrence, including all islands nearest to the said county and wholly or in part opposite to the same;

From those two statutes in both Upper Canada and Lower Canada, which were afterwards included in the consolidated statutes of the province of Ontario and later the province of Quebec, it became quite clear that the boundary was in the middle of the channel. The point was: Where was the channel? That was the difficult point.
After representations had been made by the federal government to the respective provinces a commission was established to inquire where the middle of the stream was or in other words where the boundary line lay between the two provinces. The commissioner for the province of Ontario, Mr. Rorke and the commissioner for the province of Quebec, Mr. Cote, in 1926, following their appointment as a commission, undertook to settle the question and together they were able to succeed in delineating the boundary on lake St. Francis from the westerly limit of the province of Ontario at Point Beaudette to a point about 300 miles south of Ross island. Beyond that they could not agree.
At that stage the province of Ontario suggested to the province of Quebec that they pass legislation and asked the federal government to approve it. The province of Quebec felt that that would not be the proper course. The province of Quebec said that until the whole boundary line has been delineated from Point Beaudette to the international boundary line opposite the city of Cornwall it would not be advisable to seek legislation from the federal government. However, at a later date the commission was established again and the boundary was delineated for another several miles until now an agreement has been reached between the two provinces to a point opposite what is known as Hamilton's island.
But there still remains another ten miles of boundary line to be delineated between the two provinces. There still remains also the question of having that part of the line upon which an agreement seems to be arrived at consolidated by legislation.
I bring the matter to the attention of the minister because I know of his interest in it.
I know that he will want to do what is possible within the realm of his responsibility to have the boundary agreed upon. I should say to him that for many years I have tried to have something established with reference to the line; I have not been successful and it may be that where I have failed he will be successful. I wish him every success in that respect. I understand-and I say this with all deference-that he is a close friend of the premier of the province of Quebec.

My colleague in this house, the member for Stormont, I am sure will want to add some words in due course with respect to another reason which I will not pursue at this time because I am sure he will want to do so, but there is another reason of great significance to another department of government which will also be dealt with in due course.

I mentioned a moment ago the inconvenience with which the seaway authority might find itself placed. I am not able to point to any particular inconvenience at the moment but I do know this: when the wage rates are different in one province as compared with another, when the unemployment insurance benefits and workmen's compensation benefits are different in one province as compared with another, and when many workers are engaged in work in an area which has not been demarcated, it then becomes difficult to ascertain certain facts.

That is what we in British Columbia believe, that something more is needed than just a verbal protest to Washington. In concluding my quotations I want to quote the final paragraph in this most interesting submission:
In 1952 the United States government urged Canada to expand production and increase exports to the United States by diverting from Canada's normal markets. This is brought out in the submission of the Canadian metal mining association to the United States tariff commission in November, 1953, which stated:
"In the years following world war II the demand for metals continued to grow. The competition for supplies throughout the world was such that lead and zinc were difficult to obtain, and prices reached very high levels in those countries where prices were not controlled. Even as recently as early 1952 the United States government was urging Canada to expand production and to increase exports to the United States. Even though this meant diversion from other normal markets and from markets where prices were much higher than those prevailing in the United States, Canadian producers complied at considerable financial sacrifice. The Canadian industry stood by the United States at a time when its need was stated to be urgent, and Canada is practically the only

country from which the United States is assured of supplies at all times, whether under peacetime or wartime conditions."
Now that markets and circumstances have changed somewhat in the United States that is all forgotten and there are proposals to increase tariffs that will seriously affect the mining industry in British Columbia and across Canada. I do urge the government to take courageous and strong action to meet this situation. I do not underestimate the difficulties. These problems are all complex in our modern society but I am one of the good many in this country who think it is about time that the government of Canada stood up to these people and showed them that we are not going to be pawns of the United States so far as the development of resources, trade and industry is concerned.
