Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Macleod is so inclined to stimulate his miscroscopic ego by irresponsible, irrelevant and innocuous remarks that make no impression on the Speaker, or this house. I was going to point out that a new approach on a co-operative basis had been shown and

I think that was demonstrated the other day. As the member for the constituency in which the mine is located the hon. member for Coast-Capilano gave a very good recital of the situation that exists with respect to the Britannia mining company and its employees. He explained how the price of copper had dropped, how the company was losing large sums of money, how they then discussed the matter with the employees and agreed to continue to lose a considerable sum of money per month if the employees would forego certain benefits that were due at that time under their contract.
Both the company and the employees made certain sacrifices so that the mine has continued to operate since that time. Then the price of copper fell again and created a new situation in which the losses of the company were greater than it could consider carrying for very long. The union again made a very close study of the situation and also discussed it with the management. Their first action was to call together all the British Columbia members of all parties and the matter was discussed at a meeting held in the Hotel Vancouver over a period of two days. There were members of all parties present who were all sympathetic, and I am very pleased that after the union representatives had presented their difficulties and explained the circumstances there was unanimous agreement among the members from British Columbia on a telegram to be forwarded to the government of Canada in this connection. I will not go into the exact details but they agreed in principle that this matter should receive sympathetic consideration from the government of the country.
As I said before, the situation has deteriorated further since we came to Ottawa. National officers of the union and officers of the local concerned came to Ottawa and called another meeting of British Columbia members of all parties which they gladly attended. After a further explanation of the developments and difficulties in the industry those members once again supported the representations to the meeting, later to be presented to the government. I understand that the union representatives then met some members of the cabinet who gave them a sympathetic hearing. As we heard today, the Minister of Justice when in Vancouver made a further investigation of the situation and met the management, and we understand that the matter is now under sympathetic and serious consideration by the government.
Now, Mr. Chairman, in my opinion that spirit indicates the approach that will be necessary to deal with some of these questions. I understand the Minister of Justice 96698-89J
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys met representatives of the provincial government, as well as management. It is in that spirit we are going to find solutions to these questions, through co-operation by all concerned, management, labour, the federal government and members from British Columbia. I should like to say, and I am proud to say- I think I am correct in this statement- British Columbia is the only province, the members of which from all parties, when its interests are threatened, can join together and show a common front.
This indicates an approach that can be taken to these questions. I am very pleased that this is somewhat to the discomfort of the hon. member for Macleod. In any event, in my opinion such an approach creates a better understanding of the situation and a greater appreciation of the difficulties in all persons concerned. I am sure that from this problem, from our point of view, will grow a greater appreciation of the necessity to do some planning with respect to the development of our natural resources, their utilization and investment to develop natural resources. It is in that spirit that I see a great hope in the future of doing something effective to meet this situation. This is a temporary, local situation. In the past governments have always reminded me of a forestry lookout. They see a fire and they go to try to put it out. If it rains the fire remains small. They put it out. Usually it continues to burn and does a lot of damage and goes out as a natural result of changed weather conditions; that is the attitude of most governments with respect to the economic fires in this country in the past and at this time.
I trust that this matter will continue to receive the very serious consideration of the government. I should like the minister, when he replies, to let us know what has been done in particular to meet the base metals situation, or what the government proposes. Later on, we shall look for continued favourable reports on the Britannia mine situation.

I should like to continue a subject referred to by the hon. member for Laurier, that is the demarcation of the boundary line between the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. The hon. member was quite capable of bringing this subject to the attention of the house. I am sure the information will be of value to the minister and his department. I had an opportunity of placing this subject before the house in July, 1956, when I asked the then minister of mines and technical surveys a question. In reply, the minister said as reported at page 6658 of Hansard for July 30, 1956:
I had the opportunity to see the records of the department and I find that the correspondence goes as far back as February 1938, when a series of

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys questions was placed on the order paper and answered by Hon. T. A. Crerar, then minister in charge of this department. I would refer hon. members to Hansard of May 18, 1938, page 3241.
Since I became associated with this department there has been further correspondence. On December 8, 1953, I received a letter from hon. Lionel Chevrier, then minister of transport, pointing out the urgency of having this boundary survey completed. Following receipt of his letter, I wrote to the ministers responsible for boundary survey work in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. The last paragraph of my letter reads as follows:
"You may wish to renegotiate the matter with the province of Quebec (or the province of Ontario), towards the completion of the survey for the demarcation of the line. I am fully aware that this demarcation is the entire jurisdiction of the provinces, but I simply submit that the final survey would prove beneficial to all concerned."
These letters were acknowledged, but no action was taken.
The matter of interprovincial boundary surveys is the responsibility of the provinces concerned. Our department does co-operate when a request is received from both provinces, usually by appointing the surveyor general as chairman of a three-man commission with a representative from each province; who are charged with the responsibility of completing the survey. The costs of such surveys are shared equally by the two provinces concerned and this government.
I can assure my hon. friend that, as soon as requests are received from the provinces of Ontario and Quebec for the completion of this boundary survey, our department will act immediately.
That was the stand of the former government in this matter. I took up this question with the hon. member for the county of Huntingdon in Quebec and the hon. member for Glengarry in Ontario. At that time I was assured of their entire co-operation. However, to this date no steps have been taken to bring this matter to a head. I feel it is very important. As the hon. member mentioned a little while ago, we should be interested as trustees of the department of Indian affairs because of the islands in that district. We, in the county of Stormont are not immediately affected by this boundary line because it touches the county of Glengarry. Our concern arises because many of our people go there as summer residents to enjoy the beautiful view of lake St. Francis and the fishing and hunting that the district has to offer. We find it very inconvenient, because at no time do we know whether we are in the province of Quebec or Ontario. Two years ago the game wardens on both sides of the river were having a field day bringing people to court for hunting or fishing in one province or the other.
You can see, Mr. Chairman, it is quite important that this matter should be settled once and for all. I think that with the new look in this house the government might be able to influence the provincial governments to come to an understanding on this point. As was mentioned earlier, we were concerned in this matter because of the department of
IMr. Lavigne.]
Indian affairs, because of our fish and game laws and because of the development of the St. Lawrence seaway. Recently we have been concerned because of the great activity in the area around the city of Cornwall, the eastern limits of which are on the western boundary of the county of Glengarry. The city is expanding rapidly and its very active industrial commission is extending its operations into the county of Glengarry. Recently we had the opening of the Edo manufacturing plant, just east of the city of Cornwall.
What I am concerned with is the development of a harbour in that area, something which will bring about a serious problem if this question of boundary line is not settled. The city of Cornwall will spread to the east into the county of Glengarry but to the south it will touch the province of Quebec. We in the county of Stormont would be very happy if some action were taken in this matter. I hope the minister will use his influence with his party and his good offices to bring the two provincial governments to an understanding on this boundary line question.

Mr. Chairman, first of all may I assure the hon. Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Comtois) that I would be the last in this house who would want to embarrass him in any way. The trepidation-or should I say the fear-which was gripping me when I found myself for the first time in the same situation in 1954, is still much too fresh in my memory.
I rise to speak at this stage in the debate because I believe I should bring up a matter which, at the present time, is extremely important as regards the rights of the provinces to crown lands. In order to explain the problem more clearly, I should like first of all, to give some background information, and to be allowed to continue my remarks in English for that purpose.
(Text):
The act respecting the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys is chapter 73 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952. Section 5 thereof reads as follows:
The duties, powers and functions of the minister extend to and include all matters over which the parliament of Canada has jurisdiction relating to mines, minerals, explosives and technical surveys.
Under section 7 the minister has a degree of responsibility for the demarcation of boundary lines between the various jurisdictions in Canada.
Earlier this session I had placed on the order paper a series of questions relating to the seabed and subsoil under territorial waters in Canada. The replies to the questions I asked can be found at page 1169 of Hansard. One of the questions was with regard to the

crown rights in Hudson bay. The question reads as follows:
1.	Are the waters of Hudson bay Canadian waters?
2.	If so, are the seabed and subsoil of Hudson bay the property of the crown (a) in the right of Canada; (b) in the right of Canada, Manitoba, Ontario and Quebec; (c) if the answer to (b) is in the affirmative, what part is respectively within each jurisdiction?
The answer given by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources is as follows:
1.	Yes. The waters of Hudson bay are Canadian waters by historic title-
2.	The law officers of the crown have advised that the control and administration of the seabed and subsoil underlying Hudson bay is vested in the crown in right of Canada.
I asked a second question which was similar with regard to Hudson strait. But of course there the only province which was involved was the province of Quebec. The answer there was similar to the one I have just read. The third question was with regard to the gulf of St. Lawrence where there has been more doubt as to the question of whether the waters of the gulf of St. Lawrence are part of the Canadian territorial sea. The answer to the first question which is substantive, as to whether the waters of the gulf of St. Lawrence are Canadian waters, is as follows:
1.	On February 8, 1949, shortly before the union of Newfoundland with Canada, the then prime minister (Mr. St. Laurent) made the following statement (Hansard-page 368) :
"We intend to contend, and I hope to be able to get acquiescence in the contention that the waters west of Newfoundland constituting the gulf of St. Lawrence shall become an inland sea-
The then prime minister continued along the same line, after which the answer goes on as follows:
The government sees no reason for departing from the principle enunciated in this statement.
On the question about the gulf of St. Lawrence which I had asked in the second part of the question, whether the seabed and -subsoil were the property of the government of Canada or whether they were the property of the government of Canada, the governments of Quebec, Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, the answer was as follows:
2.	According to international law the seabed and subsoil under the territorial sea is vested in the littoral state. The law officers of the crown have advised that the administration and control of the seabed and subsoil of the territorial sea is vested in the crown in right of Canada.
Of course, as to the question of whether the waters of the gulf of St. Lawrence, of Hudson bay and of Hudson strait should be considered by Canada as Canadian waters, as part of our territorial sea, I am in full accord with the answers given. But Canada
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys is a federal state and even if, according to international law, the seabed and subsoil of what is now recognized as the territorial sea -to the three-mile limit-is the property of the littoral state, the question of knowing whether this property pertains to the federal government or to the government of the province concerned is a matter to be decided in Canada itself, according to our constitutional law and constitutional practice and the jurisprudence of our tribunals. So I was much concerned when I received these answers, especially the second part of them, in particular the one about the gulf of St. Lawrence, which reads as follows:
The law officers of the crown have advised that the administration and control of the seabed and subsoil of the territorial sea is vested in the crown in right of Canada.
I was concerned for a number of reasons. I remember studying-and I hope my memory serves me rightly-the decisions of the privy council in the cases of the Montreal harbour commission and in that case which is known across Canada as the fisheries case. If my memory serves me aright, I repeat, the decision of the privy council as to the seabed even under tidal waters was pretty much to the contrary of the opinion expressed by the law officers of the crown. Moreover, it has been the custom in the gulf of St. Lawrence for the Department of Public Works of this government to seek and to obtain the transfer of what are known as waterlots whenever the Department of Public Works wishes to build wharves in the gulf of St. Lawrence.
If as is said in this opinion of the law offices of the crown the crown in the right of Canada is the owner of the seabed and subsoil, why should this government seek and obtain from the provincial government of Quebec the transfer of the seabed which they need for the building of their wharves. Moreover, if it is true, as the law officers of the crown say, that the seabed and subsoil in the territorial sea are under the control and administration of the crown in the right of Canada, how is it that the government of Nova Scotia has always had the control and administration over the coal mines off the shores of Cape Breton? These mines are under the territorial sea, of course, or within what is called the subsoil of the territorial sea.
I was therefore greatly concerned with that answer and I wondered if this government was not in the process of depriving the provinces of the ownership of thousands, or even hundreds of thousands, of square miles of property in Canada. I do not affirm one way or the other but I wish to draw this

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys grave problem to the attention of one of the ministers who has some responsibility for it.
I know that in the subsoil of Hudson's bay, just off the shore of the province of my hon. friend and just west of the coast of Ungava, great mineral riches have been discovered. According to the opinion given by the law officers of the crown, the nickel and iron ore discovered there would be the property of the government of Canada.
I know the hon. minister has always professed to be a great defender of provincial rights; I know this because I listened to him during the last electoral campaign and I have heard his parliamentary assistant say the same thing. I hope they will take up this matter with the law officers of the crown and with their colleagues in the cabinet and will see to it that this opinion is not simply given "off the cuff". I also hope the hon. minister will be able to secure, overnight, an opinion from those law officers explaining and substantiating, with the constitution and with the jurisprudence, that opinion which is mentioned in the answers I have received. As I said, this is a grave problem, and I know the members of this house would not like to have a question of this kind settled merely by some opinion of law officers of the crown. They would wish that the cabinet and the parliament should deal with such a matter. I sincerely believe that the provinces should be consulted with regard to it before any final decision is taken and before any final delineation is made between the boundaries of the jurisdictions of the federal government on the one hand and of the various interested provinces on the other; that is to say those provinces interested in Hudson's bay, Hudson's strait, the gulf of St. Lawrence and the seabed and subsoil of the territorial seas just off our Atlantic and Pacific shores.
I believe I have said enough to impress the minister and the members of the cabinet with the importance of this subject and I hope when he answers he will be able to deal with this matter or, if he cannot deal with it tonight, that he will be able to study it overnight and deal with it tomorrow when we resume the study of these estimates.

maintopic: THE ROYAL ASSENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise to
speak about the estimates of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys and I do so having in mind some doubts and hesitations with respect thereto. These estimates were not satisfactory to many parts of Canada when the Liberals introduced them a year ago and I think, because no changes have been made, they still would not be acceptable in many respects today.

I come from a riding in the northern part of Ontario which has a very large mining area. You may know of the Kerr-Addison mine near Larder Lake, which is the largest gold mine in Canada and one of the largest on the continent. We have many other mines in Timiskaming which make up the Kirkland lake gold mining area and one of the very important gold mining fields. This area is well-known across the world. The problem with respect to gold is one of many facing the mining industry today and probably more difficult to solve than any other. We are continually faced in the gold mining industry with the need for an increase in the price of our products. That price is paid as a result of an agreement entered into between Canada and the United States of America a number of years ago. The mines have had to provide for the price of commodities purchased for their operation and we have had to keep in line with the cost of living, but we have found that the price for our product remains the same however as it was in the depression days.
With respect to this department an act was passed called the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. This act has been responsible to some extent for the maintenance and even the very existence of some of our mines. I would just like to refer to what the present Minister of Finance had to say in discussing the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act on June 12, 1956 as recorded on page 4972 of Hansard. He said:
I have emphasized, sir, that this measure is no solution of the deep-seated problem of the gold mining industry. The difficulty and the flaw in measures of this kind is that they often lull the government and lull parliament into thinking that the problem has been solved, or at least that the problem has been met for the time being. No hon. member should delude himself into thinking that this measure is any solution, even on the short-run basis, of the needs and the problems of the gold-mining industry. These problems are going to require much more far-sighted solutions than are offered by the hand-to-mouth, stop-gap type of assistance that we have in the present measure.
Therefore, I say I am surprised that this type of legislation should have been reintroduced and that these estimates should not have been corrected to take into consideration the previous thinking of the present Minister of Finance.
We should look at some of the communities which have depended on gold mining assistance. Take two examples which were originally under E.G.M.A. in 1948 when it was introduced, the Young Davidson Mine, a subsidiary of the Hollinger Gold Mine of Timmins and, secondly, the Matachewan Consolidated Mines, both of Matachewan. These mines did receive assistance. Today there is nobody in those towns. A wonderful example

is Matachewan. We had a community with a population of 4,000 or 5,000, having schools both public and separate, a fire department, hospitals, police force-completely equipped as a modern town-yet because of the limited assistance which has been paid under E.G.-M.A. these towns are now ghost towns and no people are working in the mining industry in those areas. We have not solved the problem of those communities or even tried to solve it.
Why, I should like to ask, are we interested in gold? I think that gold itself, as a commodity, has absolutely no value except as a means of adornment. If we want to make jewelry out of it, well and good. But the countries of the world when they signed the Bretton Woods agreement and set up the international bank set it up on the basis of a gold standard. We in turn in 1946 agreed to stabilize our gold price at $35 in relation to 13.71 grains of fine gold U.S., so that if we do not want to carry gold about in our pockets we have, to some extent, to support this legislation dealing with our financial affairs.
Personally, I am not too much interested in the gold. What I am interested in is what gold has done for this country. In 1909, or thereabouts, when gold was found in northern Ontario it had the same effect that the discovery of gold had in California; it spearheaded the development of that part of the country. Those young towns were built around the gold mining industry, and if that industry did nothing else it opened up the north of this province and created the communities we now find there. It was responsible, too, for the industries which are dependent on gold mining.
The problem of gold prices was faced when we agreed that if the price of gold was not to change, then emergency gold mining assistance should be paid. I think this assistance must be given, and that it must be increased, not decreased as it has been over the past few years under the former Liberal government. I think it has to be increased to take care of the needs of the communities in which gold is mined. The federal government has shown consideration to the gold mining industry in a number of ways. First, it pays a subsidy if mines cannot produce economically; secondly, it has allowed the gold mining industry three years in which to bring a new producing mine into production, without charging any income tax; and, thirdly, it has allowed gold mines to speed up the amortization of their depreciation. I think it is now time that we should take a further look at the E.G.M.A. whose provisions, as the Minister of Finance has said, were to be only a temporary stop gap.
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
I should like to suggest that this assistance be increased, but that it be increased with reservations. First, I should like to see E.G.M.A. assistance paid only to mines that need it. I know of some cases where this is not done, because I worked underground in a gold mine for 15 years and I know something about the situation. I am sure the Canadian people have heard of high-grading of gold. Somebody gets away with a few dollars of high-grade and it makes a good story in the newspapers. But many of these mines are being "low-graded". There are high grades in stopes which are shut off, and as a result the Canadian people are financing the production of low grade ore at a time when there is this other ore which would bring profits.
There are, of course, companies which need this assistance in order to be able to carry on at all. I strongly suggest that if this government is interested in increasing employment it should consider spending a few more dollars under the E.G.M.A. for the sake of reemploying a large number of people who have been thrown out of work by the closing down of marginal mines. But if we are going to pay under this E.G.M.A., then I think the Canadian people should insist that the money should go, first of all, to the people who work in the industry, because they are all underpaid at the present time in relation to other hard rock miners. Some, at least, of this assistance should be earmarked for the people who produce the gold.
Machines have been introduced and automation has been brought into the mines as well as elsewhere, and production has risen beyond the expectations that one might have expected from increased wages, but still, this increase which I suggest under the E.G.M.A. should also be paid in such a way that a percentage of it at least should go directly into the communities which are totally dependent on this emergency assistance. Surely if there is anything left over by way of profit, a reasonable amount should be retained locally, but some of these mines are taking the amount that is paid them under the E.G.M.A. and paying an equivalent amount to the shareholders, with the effect that the Canadian people are paying dividends to the shareholders.
According to the estimates, there are inspectors, federal inspectors. In my 15 years underground I never met a federal government inspector. They may exist, but I never met one. If there are any, I suggest they should take a look at this situation in relation to the amount of ore that is held in reserve, the veins that ore is in, and the

13S4
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys assay value of that ore, so that we may ensure a much more honest practice than we have at the present time.
We have a large number of other mines which are closed because they cannot operate at a profit. Many of these are in the Kirkland lake area, and in each case the miners who lost their employment were not absorbed in other enterprises in the communities and had to leave those communities which, in turn, were dependent upon them. If we are going to continue the E.G.M.A.-and I say it has to be continued because we have no alternative at the present time-then we should insist on the requirements I have mentioned, namely that the needs of the miners and the needs of the communities should be met before any money is "divvied" out to anybody else. We have miners working in those mines who have no future. They have no pensions put away for their future. I suggest that some of this money could be used for government assistance to set up a national pension plan for mining and allied industries.
The Canadian people have had a great deal of benefit from miners, probably more from them than they have received from any other class of people in Canada. We And-and I think this can be borne out and has been borne out thousands of times in the past-that we have been able to develop the uranium fields which are so important to the Canadian people today because we have had miners who worked in the hard-rock mining industry for a number of years. It is possible to take one skilled miner and put four unskilled miners with him, but it is impossible to take all unskilled miners and expect to get a mine in operation. The fact that these miners have been able to move from the gold-mining fields into the copper fields of Gaspe, into Belle-Isle in Newfoundland, into the uranium fields in Elliott lake, the new property in Moak lake and the iron industry in the new Helen mining area is proof that hard-rock gold miners who spent their lifetime in the gold-mining industry are easily adaptable.
The industry is very important to the Canadian people because of its flexibility. One of the reasons why it is flexible is that we have the type of people who are willing to make the sacrifice to move from one job where they have security into a pioneering field. If we are to recognize this fact, then we should implement, with some assistance from the federal government at least in the administration of a pension plan. We should institute industrial portable pensions which will cover miners so that they can move from mine to mine and field to field, and

still at the end of 20 years be able to retire on some kind of pension.
I am told that not too many miners last more than 20 years in the mines. We have a high mortality rate. Silicosis, heart trouble and all types of pulmonary diseases are prevalent, and some assistance should be given in that respect. I strongly urge that the new government take into consideration this matter of portable pensions for this industry. I should also like to say that of the hundreds of mines that are opened up every year very few exist long enough for industrial pensions under any other scheme.
In Timiskaming we have a number of other problems in the mining field. I think the gold-mining industry is of prime importance to the country. Because of the statements the Minister of Finance has made in the house over the years he must go out and effectively and very vocally ask for an increase in the price of gold from our United States buyers. On a number of occasions in recent years we have seen South Africa, Australia, yes and even France, ask for an increase in the price of gold and Canada has stayed quietly back and let somebody else do it. I think it is time, particularly in the light of what the minister has said over the years, that he take the lead in trying to increase the price of gold because that is the only solution on a long-term basis of this problem.
In my riding we have a number of people going into the uranium fields of Blind River. I would like to suggest to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys that some consideration be given to those people because I can see exactly the same problem developing in the uranium fields of Elliott Lake as developed elsewhere. Frankly, I am surprised that we have not heard the representative from that area say something about it. We are hearing today, and we have heard it in recent years, that there are short-term contracts in the Elliott Lake area. We are asking the miners to leave northern Ontario to go into those areas and we are finding that they are being asked to build houses. The National Housing Act will cover them for a period of five years, which is the length of the uranium contracts. From then on there is a kind of half-baked deal between the mining companies and the employees to continue payments for 20 years. I am suggesting that some consideration be given to those people, because I think they are being taken in on the same kind of deal that my friends in the Matachewan area were taken in on, where, after they worked in the industry for 10 years or 15 years, spent their lives there, put all their money into housing and

into the community, found that there was no more occupation for them in that industry.
I would suggest that some of the money given as emergency gold mining assistance be taken and put into secondary industries. Secondary industries could be put into northern Ontario if they do not have to pay any federal taxes for three years, if they could write off their complete depreciation in 10 years and still get a handout besides to help them get their original start. We are going to have secondary industries in northern Ontario and then Kirkland Lake will be a booming community instead of just holding its own. I think we have that obligation, not only to Kirkland Lake, Larder Lake, Matach-ewan and Cobalt, but to all the other towns that are dependent on mining because, no mattef'ywhat we do about mining, there will come a day when there will be no more minerals of any quantity, or no worthwhile value, in that rock. Secondary industries must be developed to carry on the continuity of those communities which are hard to build up.
Let me mention Cobalt. I think it is a wonderful example because Cobalt certainly was a great old town. Everybody has seen the sign, or heard of it-if they have not they should go up and see the sign which reads, "Where all the silver comes from". We have seen a boom and bust in the silver market over the years. I have seen Cobalt when you could buy a shack for $10,000 and the next month you could buy the best house in town for $500. We have seen the ups and downs of Cobalt. Nothing has ever been done to stabilize the market for those products.
We have heard some discussion on zinc and copper and I think silver comes in that category; certainly this new metal cobalt comes in that category. I was very surprised to find that last spring the cobalt market had disappeared. There had been a long-term proposition but cobalt could be obtained much cheaper from the Belgian Congo. Is it the desire of the people of Canada to go to the Belgian Congo to buy our cobalt when we have a vast quantity of it already in Ontario and in Canada? I do not think so. Cobalt is necessary as a strategic war material. It is a metal that keeps; it can be stockpiled effectively. It does not deteriorate. We could pile it up in a yard some place and still maintain the cobalt; but we would not be able to get cobalt tomorrow if there was a need for it because there is no development of the cobalt veins in the Cobalt area. The cobalt is there.
But because the mining companys knew it was only a short-term contract, that it was going to run out in a certain period, they said, "Why in thunder should we block out a new supply of cobalt? Development work costs
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys money." Why should they block it out? Because this is free enterprise, and I do not disagree that maybe this is the way they should run it, then we are in this position. We have need for the strategic war metal, cobalt, tomorrow-and the committee should know that cobalt is used in the manufacture of new types of metal. It is used in magnetos; it is used in all steel that is going to be used in very high temperatures and I presume that even in the missile program, which we may or may not be developing, this type of metal is very necessary. If we are going to spend the amounts of money that we as Canadians believe should be spent in this direction then it would be a lot cheaper to do it here than waiting until the need is much greater. If we believe that then we have to do the development work needed because it takes time.
In the meantime this community is existing on a boom and bust economy and I do not think that is the desire of the Canadian people. It certainly is not producing any wealth for the farming community because when people are living on relief you would be surprised how little good beef they buy and how little butter they buy. The farming communities close by are not doing any selling. In my opinion there should be further assistance for these mining communities in the estimates.
Near Kirkland Lake we have a very large iron deposit. It has been drilled and its potentiality has been ascertained. The necessary magnetometer surveys have been made. The amount of ore is very extensive, but what do we find has happened? The same thing has happened as in the case of a great many of our natural resources. Control of the property has fallen into the hands of United States interests. At the present time they have no need to develop the property. I think the Canadian people need that industry developed. I am sure that the people of Kirkland Lake and Dane need that industry developed, and I suggest that something should be done to assist in its initial development. In my opinion the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys has done very little in this regard.
We also have a field of coal in that immediate area which would be a great asset in furthering the development of secondary industries another phase of industry which would help to build up the communities in these areas. There is a large lignite deposit but some money is needed for its development and the establishment of a pilot plant so that we may know exactly how we can get the heat and energy from the coal. This is also something that should be developed under the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys.

Will he amend the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act, the administration of which comes under his department, to make provision that when a mine receives assistance a percentage of that assistance will automatically go into the salaries and wages of the employees in the industry and into a pension plan for their retirement? Mr. Chairman, I propose, as always, to be extremely brief. I should like to say a word in general about the estimates of the department and perhaps comment, and nothing more, on the predicament of what is Canada's largest mineral industry, the petroleum industry. As to the estimates I should like first of all to do something that is perhaps unusual with respect to a government department. As one who comes from the practical side of the industry I should like to congratulate the service or field personnel, particularly those men of the department of geology and geophysics who have for some time now assisted the development of the resources of our country, at times under rather difficult conditions. When I look at the department, Mr. Chairman, the only point which concerns me is whether or not we have taken into consideration the expansion of the development of resources in Canada. I notice that there is actually a drop in the number of geologists. I also notice that the amount of money we are making available to universities for exploration and research has not altered at all.
I think we should remember that what has made our country economically sound has been the exploitation and development of both natural and human resources. I believe we will agree that when we consider these estimates we are dealing with one of the most important departments of government, one which has been treated to some extent in the past as a poor relation of government.
I am going to make two suggestions to the minister. The first has to do with personnel. I do not know how he can expect to retain his staff of technicians having regard to the salaries that these men are receiving from the department. We are going to have to meet the competition of companies involved in the development of our resources. I happen to know something of the replacement of staff in this department. I happen to know also that it is not the


intention of the government to try to compete with industry because it is expected that industry will naturally be a higher bidder. But when we expect these men to carry out this important task for us, we must recognize that they are going to have to have salaries comparable certainly to the amount of work they are doing for the department.
The other point to which I should like to make reference is one which the minister undoubtedly will have to discuss with the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, one which has not hitherto been a problem. I refer to the natural resources underlying the national parks of Canada. It is a fact, of course, that there is no resource development of any national park in that sense. Naturally it is not expected that we should immediately open gold mines or oil wells in national parks, but I think we are going to have to recognize that certain areas of our parks represent vast natural wealth under the surface.
It is in this department that the leases or rights are held and therefore there must be some consideration of a future policy between the two departments with respect to whether or not these areas are going to be developed or on what basis they are going to be dealt with. Unquestionably the government is today losing money by way of royalties which they could well use.
I am going to close by referring to something that it was my privilege to deal with in the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I mentioned at that time the problem facing the oil industry, particularly in Alberta but also in western Canada generally. I do not like repetition and I do not intend to bore hon. members with the details. The fact of the matter is that every columnist from one end of Canada to the other has commented on the matter and I could do no more than repeat what they have said. Suffice it to say that the problem we have encountered in western Canada with respect to oil development is fast reaching a crisis in that a depressed industry is in a situation which is going to require assistance, not in the form of subsidies but in the form of intelligent planning with the aid of the federal and provincial governments. I have already expressed my views on how this can best be done and I will not repeat them here.
Perhaps some hon. members may look upon this industry, as is so often the case, as an industry involving only wealthy men and wealthy provinces. Let me reassure you that, while perhaps it is difficult to plead a case for Alberta which gives $20 to a number of its residents from oil dividends, there are still in Alberta a great many young

men and women who today are without work because of the depressed state of that industry. Better than half of the drilling crews are today unemployed. Better than half of the exploration crews are today without work. Consequently, those auxiliary servicing crews that keep them in the field are also suffering.
I cannot help but feel a little frustrated, not with my own party but with the whole area of this eastern section of Canada which, when you complain bitterly about the depressed state of the oil industry, they say to you, you will now be short a few millionaires and they are going to have to get by with last year's Cadillacs. I remind you that a great many of our people, a substantial part of our population, are dependent on this industry. They realize that some action must be taken soon. I am going to sit down after saying this. This industry, which is so vitally affected by the department of mines and of course the geological surveys, has been given a great deal of assistance in many fields by the department, such as the development to some extent of the tar sands which represent the largest known oil reserves in the world. It has given us assistance in setting up what is now known as the mines ministers conference, an organization designed to bring uniformity into the laws on gas and oil in Canada. It has given us assistance through technicians and help in developing better methods for exploring for oil and gas. I am going to suggest, therefore, that a proper lead from government in aiding the oil and gas industry today and in relieving some of the problems that they have, rest with the minister of mines. I hope he will give this his consideration.

In speaking about the unemployment situation on Tuesday afternoon, Mr. Chairman, I made reference to the critical situation that is developing in the lead and zinc industry. The hon. member for Kootenay West and the hon. member for Villeneuve made extensive references to that problem this afternoon. While prices are greatly depressed at this time, we are facing a much more serious situation in the threat of higher tariffs being imposed by the United States. The mine, mill and smelter workers brief, to which reference was made this afternoon by the hon. member for Kootenay West, points out just what may take place if these proposed tariffs are imposed. The union maintains a rather intensive research department in their head office in Toronto, and they have gone to some lengths to show just what the situation is with respect to these base metals.
There is a minimum of fabrication within Canada, so the major part of the Canadian
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys production of lead, zinc and copper is exported. The brief goes on to say that about 80 per cent of the lead, 60 per cent of the copper and over 90 per cent of the zinc is exported. I should think about 50 per cent of the economy of both the east and west Kootenays depends on these base metals, especially lead and zinc. If this proposed tariff were imposed, one can see what would happen. While our market would not be wiped out entirely, it would undoubtedly mean large lay-offs and the curtailment of the industry generally. About two-thirds of our zinc production and over 40 per cent of our lead production is exported to the United States. The proportion of our copper and zinc production going to the United States has been rising quite rapidly. I know that the minister of mines cannot be responsible for any action that may be taken by United States authorities, but I hope he will impress upon the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister the urgency of this matter so that they will make even stronger representations to the United States than they appear to be doing at this time.
There is another matter that seems to be affecting the mining industry of British Columbia. While it seems to be a purely provincial matter, I believe the federal government does enter into the picture. Some time ago I asked the Minister of Justice to look into bill No. 87, introduced by the provincial government. This bill provides for a tax on minerals of 25 to 50 cents on every ton of ore that is being mined for export. This provision seems to me to be a violation of section 2 of the British North America Act under which the federal government is responsible for the trade of our nation. The bill was introduced for the specific purpose of preventing, in so far as this restriction is able, the export of iron ore from British Columbia. The mining industry itself fears the extension of this legislation to cover other metals. Undoubtedly this fact has had something to do with the depression in the mining industry in British Columbia. The bill has been on the statute books since the last session of the legislature, but was only invoked some few weeks ago.
I know that the Minister of Justice has been very busy, but I am sure he is looking into this matter. I hope the minister of mines also will take the matter into consideration. Undoubtedly the measure was introduced into the provincial legislature in good faith, but the representatives of the mining industry view it with great apprehension. The hon. member for Calgary South has shown his dissatisfaction with what is taking place in the oil and gas industries. I think

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys if he were to look about him he would find amongst his own colleagues people who have done more to contribute to the depressed state of the gas and oil industries in Alberta than any other group in this house or in all of Canada.
Surely the need for gas sales and gas export would be one thing that would depress the development of the oil and gas industry in that province. I understand that the premier of the province came to Ottawa only recently to make his representations to the Prime Minister in order to see if he would not do something to assure that gas may be exported and marketed in the United States under commitments given by the previous government. I hope that we are not going to find, after the next 15 years or 20 years, that we are left with enough gas in the ground to provide fuel for the next thousand years, as is the condition of the coal industry in Alberta and British Columbia. Had we taken, when coal was first being exported the attitude that seems to be taken over natural gas, those who opposed the export would have looked very silly indeed today. Atomic energy and fuel may soon displace even gas and oil.
But I am sure that the province of Alberta itself has made a thorough study of its reserves. The gas conservation board has been in operation for many years. If they have satisfied themselves

and they are responsible to the people of the province-that they have an unlimited supply ready for sale, we should not attempt to prevent the action they wish to take. I might say again to the hon. member that I think he knows probably as well as does anyone that it has been the attitude of his party that has very seriously affected the gas and oil industry in Alberta.

Mr. Chairman, in rising to speak at this time I unfortunately have not the experience of the hon. member for Villeneuve who has had many years of experience in this house and who possibly has had time, as I have not, since this house opened to do some research and study on the mining picture as a whole across this country. I have found that the first month of a new member's time in this house is taken up mostly in finding where to look for what he is looking for. However, tonight I should like to deal with one specific aspect of the mining situation in Canada, one with which I am very familiar. I refer to the situation of the gold mining area in northern Ontario, with particular reference to the communities which are dependent on those gold mines, as was outlined so well by the hon. member for Timiskaming.
I should like to go back a few years to the time when I first arrived in the gold mining area of Timmins. It is necessary to go back to 1934. Possibly there are in this house hon. members whose memory does not go back that far. In fact, I think there may be one or two hon. members in this house who were born just about that time. That was in the middle of the days that have often been referred to as the "dirty thirties". I would not go so far as some hon. members have gone and refer to them as the former days or in fact the last days of the Conservative government. However, those were the days of the depression. Those were the days when men were travelling across this country from coast to coast. They were slandered. They were thrown in jail. They were called hoboes and everything else when, in fact, all they were-the biggest part of them-were merely people looking for a job and not knowing where to find it.
I recall arriving in Timmins in the summer of 1934. I will admit I was quite young at the time. However, during times of depression if you are big enough, you are old enough; and that is the situation in which I found myself. I recall that at that time before you could get a steady job in Timmins you had to overcome competition because there were in the neighbourhood of 5,000 and 10,000 men in the same position that I was in, who had come to Timmins from coast to coast because they heard that times were good in Timmins. I recall that when you could get a job as a spare-time worker they paid you 30 cents an hour up to 10 hours a day and if you worked more than 10 hours a day you were hired by the day

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
and you were paid $3 a day. That is possibly fantastic in the opinion of people in this era; they possibly find it hard to believe, being used to the trade union movement as we have developed it in this country today. However. I can assure you that my memory is very good. I could name the place where I worked and so forth and so on, but I do not think we need to waste the time of this house by going into the details.
I can also recall when I first started working underground in the Buffalo-Ankerite mines which are closed down at the present time. They are one of the victims referred to by my colleague the hon. member for Timiskaming. It was a low-grade property with a huge ore base but the mine could not meet the problems of the gold mining industry, even with the present gold mining subsidy. The management had changed just before I started to work at this property. We had a new mine captain who used to make it his brag that every day when he went underground he fired the first man he saw regardless of who he was or what he was doing just in order to smarten up the rest of them. I would ask hon. members just to think for one moment of the position of the man who happened to be first seen that day. If he had a family of ten children it never entered the picture at all. He just happened to be the unfortunate man who was to be used as an example for the rest. Actually it was a very silly thing to do because all the men used to hide behind pillars, in the shafts or any place else available so that they would not be the first man seen.
I recall when I first joined the trade union. In those days you had to go into town, circle down through a back alley, go in through a tiny little door, pay your dues, take your union button home and hide it under the shirts in the drawer of your dresser. You dare not even mention the word "union" on the job because if you did so one of the 200 men at the gate would take your job the next day. Times have changed considerably since then but unfortunately, while times change evidently problems stay right with us. Possibly the problems we had in those days are forgotten today but we have a new set of problems facing us today.
These problems were very well outlined by previous speakers; not only the problems of the gold mining industry but also the problems of the communities which those industries support. In my opinion these are knotty problems; they are not problems which can be solved overnight or at one meeting. Wages, as has been mentioned, are extremely low in the gold mines and as a result of
these low wages you will find other aspects of the community which are depressed. For example you will find rents in mining towns are very low for the simple reason that there are not as many miners there today as there were at one time. Consequently there is a surplus of houses in such places in these days of housing shortage. There are certain other aspects however which are not affected by low wages; food costs just as much up there as it does anywhere else and in northern Ontario there is an additional problem where we have higher costs for fuel as well as two extra months of winter in each year when fuel has to be used.
At the present time in the gold mining industry in Timmins negotiations are under way with all the local mines for a new collective bargaining agreement and the No. 1 item in those negotiations is the question of a pension plan. As the years have gone by we have seen, owing to the efforts of trade unions, pension plans have been established in various industries all across the country. Unfortunately, however, it seems to depend pretty well on the strength of the union as to how much is accomplished in this respect.
I can think of no industry in Canada from coast to coast which needs a pension plan more than the mining industry. There is no mercy in hard rock; if you are working underground and you have an accident you must remember that you are dealing with hard rock. That is why we see such a high incidence of lost-time accidents in gold mines; that is why gold miners have to pay an additional premium for their life and accident insurance policies. The insurance companies from their records recognize the fact that the gold mining industry is a very hazardous one. Added to that is the deadly, creeping threat of silicosis. Possibly it is not necessary to explain to this house that silicosis is not a disease, as many people think; it is merely a condition into which the lungs of miners degenerate after long service in the mines. It is just a series of scar tissues formed on the lungs from this silica dust which eventually prevents the lungs from expanding as they normally should. This brings about a general deterioration of the system until such time as the mirier succumbs. I think I noted at one time the average age of a gold miner's life is 54 years as against the national average of about 67 years.
This condition brings about a situation where the miner is no longer able to carry on his duties and, as so well outlined by the hon. member for Timiskaming, we have no secondary industries in the gold mining communities which might absorb these older members at such times. That is why it is
1400	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys so important that pensions should be established for this industry. This has a very pertinent bearing on the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act which is considered with respect to the estimates of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys.
There is another aspect with which I would like to deal and that is the situation in respect to collective bargaining between the gold miners and the gold mine operators. I think this possibly ties in with the old picture of why this gold mining problem and this Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act has been such a problem. If these mines were small local properties then the problem would not be so difficult; they would either be paying propositions or they would not and they could be judged and dealt with accordingly. But we find the situation is far different from that. We find most of these mines are subsidiaries of vast, national, international, and in some cases intercontinental corporations.
Last summer I was able to obtain the financial report of one of our local mines which showed a profit on the local property of about $98,000. In addition it received a gold mining subsidy under the act of $385,000. However, they had charged the costs of development work done at oil properties against the local property and showed an overall loss of $28,000. That is just one aspect of the problems which are all mixed up in this Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act.
We also have to consider the fact that some mining operators today are the only people in Canada who absolutely refuse to co-operate with the trade union movement in any way, shape or form.
In my remarks some weeks ago during the debate on the speech from the throne I made reference to the situation in Murdochville, Quebec during this last summer. I do not think I need to go into the details here because I am quite sure hon. members are familiar with that situation. I mentioned also at that time that the same people who operate Murdochville either own or have controlling interest in five of the 11 mines in the Timmins area today. It follows therefore that the same mental attitude toward the trade union movement and collective bargaining which was displayed this summer in Murdochville will in all probability be carried into the gold mining communities in the Porcupine camp.
I would like to submit that this situation cannot be solved, in fact it cannot be even understood through a meeting with either one side or the other. If you meet with management you get management's side of the picture; if you meet with the unions you get


the other side of the picture. I would like to suggest therefore that the only way to get a proper picture of the gold mining situation in Canada today, with all its problems, is for this house to take the lead by setting up a committee consisting of federal, provincial, and municipal authorities, plus representatives of management and union. That committee could go into all aspects of the gold mining industry and bring out a report, giving this house the true picture so that we will know how to take the necessary sensible and responsible steps with regard to E.G.M.A.
There is one other matter I would like to mention. In 1941 there were 28 gold mines operating in the Timmins area; today there are 11. In addition the Hollinger Consolidated Gold Mines in 1941 employed about
3,000	men while today they get a similar tonnage with about 1,100 men.
This might seem at the moment just a problem relating to the town of Timmins, or to the gold mining municipalities dependent on the gold mines, but I should like to bring to the attention of hon. members that some 126 communities in the province of Ontario are instrumental in supplying the needs of these gold miners. In one community they make the safety rubber boots that the miners wear; in another place they make the tracks on which they run the cars, and in another they make the machines. There are 1001 other things which are supplied to the miners which are not made in the gold mining communities, but in Toronto, Hamilton, Windsor, Kingston and London. So, if the gold mines go, not only are those communities directly affected but the repercussions are going to be felt right across the country. That is one thing which makes this a problem not only for the gold mines and the gold mining communities but also for hon. members of this house from one end of the country to the other, and certainly it is a problem for the government about which, Mr. Chairman, I submit it should use every effort to do something.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word or two about the gas and oil industries in the province of Alberta. One of the conditions which I think is contributing very largely in our part of the country to an ever-rising unemployment problem is the lack of employment in these industries and in the coal industry. These industries are three of the largest in the west, and they are three which are most affected as far as the gas industry is concerned. I want to agree with the hon. member for Kootenay East who said a while ago that this government must accept a large share of the responsibility for the depressed condition of

the gas industry in the province of Alberta. Those of us who were here last year will quite well recall the outstanding effort-and I emphasize the word "outstanding"-which was made by the Conservative party in an attempt to defeat the proposal to construct a trans-Canada gas pipe line. If they had had their way the gas industry of the province of Alberta and, eventually of Saskatchewan too, would have received a very severe set-back.
Not only did this present government do its utmost to prevent the construction of the trans-Canada gas pipe line, but they have since done considerable damage to the possibility of having gas exported to the United States. Some time ago the leader of this party, the hon. member for Peace River, asked the Prime Minister a question concerning the possibility of exporting gas to the United States, bearing in mind a commitment which was given by the former minister of trade and commerce last year, and the Prime Minister stated, in effect, that he would not accept as his responsibility any commitment made by the previous government. That has certainly gone a long way toward supplying material for those in the United States who are endeavouring to prevent the export of Alberta gas into the United States. It is certainly not helping to build our export business, and it is certainly not helping to bring United States dollars into Canada to offset our tremendous adverse balance of trade. As I say, the present government must accept a large share of responsibility for this.

November 12, 1957.
The Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker,

maintopic: ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS

speechtext:
Prime Minister of Canada,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Mr. Diefenbaker:
I am glad to learn from your letter of October 31, 1957, that all provinces have accepted November 25 and 26 as the dates for the proposed federal-provincial conference and that the conference has accordingly been called for that time.
We in Manitoba are in entire agreement with your government in believing that the conference should centre on dominion-provincial fiscal relations and that though other current issues having a bearing on the main question can be discussed, the detailed consideration of these subjects should be undertaken by groups which are directly interested in them and which can devote more time to their study than the plenary conference would likely give. One of the most important of these is hospital insurance and I would therefore like to urge again, as I did in my recent letter on the subject, that arrangements be made for a full discussion of hospital insurance, either just before or just after the federal-provincial financial conference.
My colleagues and I are somewhat concerned about the wording of your letter of October 31, 1957, particularly in view of your earlier one of September 16, 1957. It seemed clear to us in the letter of September 16 that the meeting proposed for November 25 and .26 was indeed to be a detailed conference on fiscal relations and in view of the general tenor of that letter and the matters to which it refers we expected that the provinces were being invited to a conference which would deal exhaustively with the urgent and ever-pressing problem of provincial and municipal financial requirements. One small section of your letter of October 31, however, seems to indicate that you have changed your mind about the scope of this conference. There seems to be an implication in your letter that the November conference is really to be a preliminary one.
Were this interpretation of ours, which we can hardly credit, correct, we would indeed feel that a serious change had been made in the plans for this meeting. In
giving consideration to your letter and invitation of September 16 we were impressed, as we believe many people throughout the nation are, with the urgency of the provincial and municipal financial problems as they relate to the fiscal arrangements between the various forms of government in Canada. It was in the light of these considerations that we made our plans to attend the meeting in Ottawa at that time, even though the dates were not the ones which we would have chosen. For this reason we find it difficult to think that we have been asked to make our decisions against one background only to find that the type of conference is now to be changed from a decisive one to one which, under a fairly easy interpretation of your letter of October 31, might well be of a preliminary nature only.
We are most anxious to have your reassurance that the conference to be held in Ottawa on November 25 and 26 is to be one at which significant agreements can be reached as to the adequacy or otherwise of the present fiscal relations as between the provinces and the federal government. It is, of course, recognized by all of us that the conference itself cannot decide those matters which are the prerogative of parliament and the legislatures, but we have found on previous occasions that both the federal government and the provincial governments have been able to arrive at conclusive agreements or arrangements which later on were found to be acceptable to our respective legislative bodies.
To sum up, we in Manitoba have now made our arrangements to come to the meeting in Ottawa on your suggested dates; we find ourselves in complete agreement with you that certain matters coming before the conference may well require a more specialized study than can be given to them by the conference as a whole, but we hope that your letter of October 31 does not in any way represent an intention of changing this coming conference from the decisive one which we expected from your letter of September 16, to one which has the value of only a "preliminary" meeting.
In any event Manitoba's representatives will be present, and we will expect the opportunity to place our case fully on record. We will be prepared to stay as long as is necessary in order to have full consideration given to these vitally important subjects.
Yours sincerely,
Douglas Campbell.

Dominion-Provincial Conference
Ottawa, November 17, 1957. My dear Premier:
I have your letter of the 12th and note with pleasure that you are in agreement with the federal government that the November dominion-provincial conference should center on dominion-provincial fiscal relations and that an opportunity should be afforded to discuss current issues which have a bearing on our fiscal relations. I have in mind such issues as those which bear so important a relation both to the federal budget and to provincial budgets that we cannot reach a significant agreement on changes in dominion-provincial fiscal arrangements until these issues have been carefully examined.
It is not expected that within two days it will be possible to consider fully the variety of problems and suggestions that will be put forward. The arrangements which
we have proposed are intended to make it feasible to deal seriously with the major problems. Some time will be required to consider what proposals should be made in the light of the views brought forward at the November meeting. We think it better to consider specific proposals at a subsequent meeting after we have all had an opportunity to study what is said at the first one and proposals arising from it. This need not, however, prevent our reaching agreement on any issues on which discussions next week reveal that general agreement has been achieved.
Yours sincerely,
John G. Diefenbaker.
The Honourable D. L. Campbell, M.L.A., Premier of Manitoba,
Legislative Building,
Winnipeg, Manitoba.
